tool.name: Scrapy
tool.tagline: Python framework for fast, polite, large-scale web crawling and scraping
tool.description: Scrapy is a Python framework for crawling websites and extracting structured data. You write spiders that yield requests and items, and Scrapy handles scheduling, concurrency, retries, throttling, deduplication, pipelines and export. It's the standard choice when scraping goes beyond a few pages: whole sites, recurring crawls and production data pipelines.

glossary.def: A Python framework for crawling websites: you describe which pages to visit and what data to take from them, and it handles downloading, pacing and saving.
To visit web pages automatically by following links from page to page; a crawler is a program that does this.
In Scrapy, a class you write that says which pages to start from, how to pull data out of each page, and which links to follow next.

A marker in angle brackets, like

or

, that starts or ends one piece (element) of a web page.
In HTML, a label in an element's class attribute (class="price") that groups similar elements. In Python, a class is a blueprint for creating objects.
The programming language that runs inside web browsers; pages use it to load data and change what you see after the page arrives.
In Scrapy, one record of scraped data (a dict, a scrapy.Item or a dataclass) that a spider yields; items flow through pipelines into the output.
Scrapy's built-in writing of scraped items to output files such as JSON, JSON Lines or CSV.
A query language for picking parts of an HTML or XML document by their path in the tree, like //a/@href (the href of every link).
A short pattern from CSS that picks elements on a page, like div.price (div elements with class price) or #main (the element with id main).
What response.css() and response.xpath() return in Scrapy: a list of matches you can search further or turn into strings with get() and getall().
An interactive Python prompt that Scrapy opens with a downloaded page ready in a response variable, for trying out selectors.
In Scrapy, a class whose process_item method receives every scraped item in turn, to check, clean, drop or store it.
A Scrapy helper that fills an item from selectors and runs cleaning functions on each value.
In an ItemLoader, a function chain run on each extracted value as it's added, e.g. to trim spaces or convert to a number.
In an ItemLoader, a function run once on all values collected for a field, e.g. to take the first or join them.
In Scrapy, a class plugged in between the engine and the downloader (or your spider) that sees every request and response going by and can change, replace or drop them.
A Scrapy extension that adjusts the delay between requests automatically, slowing down when a site responds slowly.
A Scrapy spider class driven by rules that say which links to follow and which pages to parse, instead of hand-written link following.
A Scrapy object that finds links in a page that match patterns you give, returning them as absolute URLs.
A function Scrapy calls instead of the callback when a request fails for good, so you can log or handle the failure.
The older Python library for event-driven networking that Scrapy is built on; it now runs on top of asyncio.
Twisted's event loop: the single loop that runs all of Scrapy's downloads and callbacks, switching between them as events happen.
Twisted's object for a result that isn't ready yet, similar to an asyncio future.
A Scrapy setting naming a folder where a crawl saves its queue and the requests it has seen, so it can be stopped and resumed.
A server program for running Scrapy spiders: you upload projects to it and start crawls through HTTP requests.
The central part of Scrapy that moves requests, responses and items between the scheduler, downloader, middlewares, spiders and pipelines.
In Scrapy, the component that holds requests waiting to be downloaded, drops duplicates and decides which goes next.
Scrapy's duplicate filter: it remembers a fingerprint of every request and drops new requests that match one already seen.
A short code Scrapy computes from a request's method, URL and body, used to recognise duplicates.
In Scrapy, a named event (spider opened, item scraped, spider closed) that extensions can subscribe to and react to.
A crawl across many websites, often not known in advance, as opposed to scraping one site.
A real web browser controlled by a program, with no window on screen; it runs a page's JavaScript so the program can read the finished page.
Structured data some pages embed in a <script type="application/ld+json"> tag, describing things like a product's name and price as JSON.
A file at the root of a website (example.com/robots.txt) that tells automated programs which parts they may and may not fetch.
Tools built into every desktop browser (right-click, Inspect) that show a page's elements, the requests it makes, and more.

concepts.name: How web pages reach your program
concepts.summary: What happens when a page is fetched: URLs, servers, HTTP requests and responses, status codes and headers, as a scraper sees them.
concepts.why: A scraper is a program that fetches pages the way a browser does, so you need to know what that exchange looks like before Scrapy automates it.
concepts.body:
When you type an address into your **browser** (Chrome, Firefox, Safari), it fetches the page from another computer and draws it for you. A scraper is a program that does the fetching part itself, then pulls the data it wants out of the page. That job is called **web scraping**.

The address is a **URL**, like `https://books.toscrape.com/catalogue/page-2.html`. It names the website (`books.toscrape.com`) and the page on it (`/catalogue/page-2.html`). Some URLs end with extra settings after a `?`, like `?page=2`.

The computer the website lives on is a **server**. Your browser or program is the **client**. They talk using **HTTP**, a simple rule book for asking and answering. The client sends a **request**: "please GET me /catalogue/page-2.html". The server sends back a **response**: the page, plus some information about it.

Every request has a **method**. **GET** means "send me this"; it's what loading a page uses. **POST** means "here's some data", and it's what a login or search form sends when you press its button.

Every response starts with a **status code**, a three-digit number saying how it went:

- `200`: OK, here's the page.
- `301` / `302`: moved; go to this other URL instead. Following it is called a redirect.
- `404`: not found. `403`: forbidden.
- `429`: too many requests; slow down. `500`–`504`: something broke on the server.

Requests and responses also carry **headers**: short labelled notes such as `Content-Type: text/html` (what kind of data this is) or `User-Agent: ...` (which program is asking). Servers can also hand the client **cookies**, small values the client stores and sends back with later requests, for example to stay logged in.

A browser sends dozens of requests per page (images, styles, data). A scraper usually needs only the page itself, or the data behind it. Scrapy automates all of this: it sends the requests, waits for the responses, and gives them to your code.
concepts.code:
# What one exchange looks like, written out as text.

# The request (client -> server):
GET /catalogue/page-2.html HTTP/1.1
Host: books.toscrape.com
User-Agent: bookbot/1.0 (+mailto:me@example.com)

# The response (server -> client):
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Set-Cookie: session=abc123

<html> ... the page itself ... </html>
takeaways: A URL names a site and a page on it
The client sends a request (GET or POST); the server sends back a response
The status code says how it went: 200 OK, 3xx moved, 4xx your problem, 5xx theirs
Headers carry extra details; cookies let a site recognise you on later requests
pitfalls: Treating any response as success; a 404 or 500 error still comes back with a page in it.

quiz.q: A scraper gets a response with status code 429. What is the server saying?
quiz.explain: 429 means the client is sending requests too fast; a polite scraper waits and slows down.

quiz.q: Which method does a browser normally use to load a page?
quiz.explain: GET asks the server to send a resource; POST is for sending data, like a submitted form.

concepts.name: Reading HTML: tags, attributes, the tree
concepts.summary: Read the HTML a server sends back: tags, elements, attributes like class and id, and how elements nest into a tree.
concepts.why: Every value a scraper extracts is found by its place in the HTML, so you need to read HTML before you can point at data in it.
concepts.body:
The page in a response is text written in **HTML**, a format that marks up content with labels saying what each piece is: a heading, a paragraph, a link, a list. Your browser reads that text and draws the page from it. The labels are **tags**: words in angle brackets. `

` opens a paragraph and `

`, with a slash, closes it. A pair of tags plus everything between them is an **element**: ```html

In stock

``` Elements sit inside other elements. A list `
    ` contains one `
  • ` element per entry, and the whole page sits inside ``, split into a `` (information about the page, such as its ``) and a `<body>` (what you see). Because of this nesting, a page forms a **tree**, like a family tree: each element has one parent and can have children. Elements with the same parent are siblings. An opening tag can carry **attributes**: extra name="value" settings. A link is `<a href="/page-2.html">next</a>`; its `href` attribute holds the URL the link goes to. Two attributes matter a lot for finding data: - `class` puts a label on elements that belong together. Every price on a shop page might have `class="price_color"`. An element can have several classes, separated by spaces. - `id` gives one element a name that is unique on the page, like `id="content"`. Some pages also run programs written in **JavaScript**, a programming language browsers understand, which can add or change content after the page has arrived. Scrapy doesn't run JavaScript: it sees only the HTML text the server sent. A later lesson covers what to do when the data you want isn't in that text. To see a page's HTML, right-click it in your browser and choose "View page source". The browser's **developer tools** (right-click, Inspect) show the same elements as a clickable tree.
concepts.code:
A Light in the ...

£51.77

  • next
takeaways: HTML marks content with tags; a pair of tags plus its content is an element
Elements nest into a tree of parents, children and siblings
Attributes like href, class and id sit inside the opening tag
Scrapy sees the HTML as sent, not what JavaScript adds later
pitfalls: Assuming everything you see in the browser is in the HTML the server sent.

quiz.q: In next, where is the URL of the next page?
quiz.explain: A link's target URL is stored in its href attribute; the text between the tags is what the reader sees.

quiz.q: What does class="price_color" on many elements tell you?
options: They are all the same element
They share a label, so you can find all of them together
quiz.explain: A class labels a group of related elements, which makes them easy to select together.

concepts.name: Projects and your first spider
concepts.summary: Create a Scrapy project, write a spider with start_urls and a parse callback, and run it with scrapy crawl.
concepts.why: Scrapy's project layout and the life of a spider are the frame every crawler you write fits into.
concepts.body:
Scraping one page is easy. Scraping a whole site means visiting thousands of pages by following links from page to page, which is called **crawling**. **Scrapy** is a **framework** for that: a larger structure where you fill in your parts and Scrapy decides when to call them.

Scrapy handles the plumbing. It downloads many pages at the same time, which is called **concurrency**. It tries a failed download again, which is called a **retry**. It also paces itself so it doesn't swamp a site, skips pages it has already visited, and saves the results. You write **spiders**: classes that say which pages to fetch and how to pull data out of each one. Reading a page's text and working out its structure is called **parsing**.

Install it with `pip install scrapy`, then in a terminal:

- `scrapy startproject bookstore` creates a project: `settings.py`, `items.py`, `pipelines.py`, `middlewares.py` and a `spiders/` package.
- `scrapy genspider quotes quotes.toscrape.com` adds a spider skeleton.
- `scrapy crawl quotes` runs the spider by its `name`.
- For a single file without a project, `scrapy runspider quotes.py` works too.

A spider is a subclass of `scrapy.Spider` with:

- `name`: a unique name used by `scrapy crawl`.
- `allowed_domains`: requests to other sites are dropped.
- `start_urls`: the first pages to fetch. To build the first requests yourself, define `async def start(self)` and yield `scrapy.Request` objects. Older code uses `start_requests()`, which current versions no longer call.
- `parse(self, response)`: the default **callback**, called with each downloaded response. It's a generator that **yields** extracted data (dicts) and new requests.

Scrapy is **asynchronous**: yielding a request doesn't download it right away. Scrapy puts it in a queue, carries on with other work, and calls your callback when the response arrives, mixed in with many other pages.
concepts.code:
# quotes.py   (run with: scrapy runspider quotes.py -O quotes.json)
import scrapy

class QuotesSpider(scrapy.Spider):
    name = "quotes"
    allowed_domains = ["quotes.toscrape.com"]
    start_urls = ["https://quotes.toscrape.com/"]

    def parse(self, response):
        self.logger.info("Visited %s (status %s)", response.url, response.status)
        for quote in response.css("div.quote"):
            yield {
                "text": quote.css("span.text::text").get(),
                "author": quote.css("small.author::text").get(),
            }

# $ scrapy startproject bookstore && cd bookstore
# $ scrapy genspider quotes quotes.toscrape.com
# $ scrapy crawl quotes
# ... 'item_scraped_count': 10, 'response_received_count': 2, ...
takeaways: startproject creates the layout; genspider adds a spider
A spider has a name, start_urls (or async start()) and parse callbacks
Callbacks yield extracted data and new requests
Requests are queued and downloaded asynchronously
pitfalls: Returning a list once at the end of parse instead of yielding results as you go (works, but delays everything and holds memory).

quiz.q: What does `scrapy crawl quotes` use to find the spider?
quiz.explain: Scrapy looks up spiders in the project by their name attribute.

concepts.name: Selectors: CSS and XPath
concepts.summary: Pull data out of responses with response.css() and response.xpath(), using ::text, ::attr(), get() and getall().
concepts.why: Selectors are how every value gets out of a page, and knowing both CSS and XPath lets you handle any structure.
concepts.body:
To point at elements, Scrapy borrows two small languages. **CSS** is the language websites use for styling, and its **selectors** pick elements: `div.quote` means "div elements with class quote", `#content` means "the element with id content", `ul li` means "li elements inside a ul". **XPath** describes a path through the tree instead: `//div[@class="quote"]/span` means "span elements directly inside a div whose class is quote".

A response offers `response.css(selector)` and `response.xpath(path)`. Both return a **SelectorList**, which you can search further or turn into strings:

- `.get()` returns the first match as a string, or `None` (or `get(default="")`).
- `.getall()` returns a list of all matches.
- `.re(r"pattern")` / `.re_first(...)` apply a **regular expression** (a pattern for text, as in Python's `re` module) to the matches.

Scrapy's CSS has two extras (from the **parsel** library) to get text and attribute values:

- `span.text::text` selects the text inside the element.
- `a::attr(href)` selects an attribute's value. Alternatively `response.css("a").attrib["href"]` reads an attribute of the first match.

XPath is more powerful for some tasks: `//a[contains(text(), "Next")]/@href` (the link whose text contains Next), `//th[text()="Price"]/following-sibling::td/text()` (the cell next to the Price label), or `string(.)` for all the text inside an element. CSS selectors are translated to XPath behind the scenes, and you can chain both: `response.css("div.product").xpath(".//h2/text()")`.

When looping over elements, search **relative** to each one: `quote.css("span.text::text")` stays inside that quote. In XPath, start the path with `.//` instead of `//` inside such a loop, which would search the whole document again.

`::text` returns only the text directly inside an element; for text spread over nested tags use `*::text` with `getall()` and join, or XPath `string()`.
concepts.code:
from scrapy.http import HtmlResponse body = b"""

Kettle steel

Price29.90 EUR
Next page
""" response = HtmlResponse(url="https://shop.example/", body=body, encoding="utf-8") p = response.css("div.product") print(p.attrib["data-sku"]) # A1 print(p.css("h2::text").get()) # 'Kettle ' print("".join(p.css("h2 *::text, h2::text").getall()).strip()) # Kettle steel print(p.xpath("string(.//h2)").get()) # Kettle steel print(p.xpath('.//th[text()="Price"]/following-sibling::td/text()').re_first(r"[\d.]+")) # 29.90 print(response.css("a.next::attr(href)").get()) # /page/2 print(response.css("span.missing::text").get(default="n/a")) # n/a
takeaways: get() for the first match, getall() for all, re()/re_first() for patterns
::text and ::attr(name) are Scrapy's CSS extras
Search relative to each element; in XPath use .// not //
XPath handles text conditions and siblings; string() joins nested text
pitfalls: Using // inside a loop over elements and getting matches from the whole page every time.

quiz.q: Inside `for q in response.css('div.quote')`, which XPath stays within q?
quiz.explain: A leading // searches from the document root; .// searches below the current node.

concepts.name: Yielding items and exporting feeds
concepts.summary: Yield dict items from callbacks and export them to JSON, JSON Lines or CSV with -O/-o or the FEEDS setting.
concepts.why: Getting clean output files without writing any export code is one of Scrapy's biggest time savers.
concepts.body:
Whatever a callback **yields** that isn't a request is treated as an **item**: one record of scraped data. It can be a dict, a Scrapy `Item`, a dataclass or an attrs object. Items flow through optional processing steps (item pipelines, a later lesson) and then into the output files Scrapy writes for you, its **feed exports**.

From the terminal:

- `scrapy crawl quotes -O quotes.json` writes (overwriting) one JSON list holding every item.
- `-o quotes.jsonl` **appends**. Use **JSON Lines** (`.jsonl`, one JSON object per line) for appending, since adding to the end of a file holding one JSON list produces an invalid file.
- `.csv` and `.xml` work too; the format follows the file extension, or force it with `-o out.txt:jsonlines`.

In code or settings, the `FEEDS` setting configures one or more outputs with options:

- `FEEDS = {"data/%(name)s-%(time)s.jsonl": {"format": "jsonlines", "encoding": "utf8"}}` uses placeholders for the spider name and the time.
- `"fields"` picks which fields go in a CSV file and in what order; `"overwrite": True` replaces existing files.
- Outputs can also go to online storage, such as Amazon S3 (`s3://bucket/key`), FTP servers or Google Cloud Storage, once the right extras are installed.

Set `FEED_EXPORT_ENCODING = "utf-8"` (the settings file of a new project already does) so accented letters like é aren't written as `\u00e9` codes in JSON.

Yield items as soon as they're extracted rather than collecting them in lists: memory use stays flat, and results are written out as you go, even if the crawl stops halfway.
takeaways: Anything yielded that isn't a Request is an item
-O overwrites, -o appends; append only to .jsonl
FEEDS configures formats, fields, paths and remote storage
Set FEED_EXPORT_ENCODING = 'utf-8' for readable JSON
pitfalls: Appending with -o to an existing .json file, producing two JSON lists stuck together in one invalid file.

quiz.q: Which output is safe to append to across multiple runs?
quiz.explain: JSON Lines has one object per line, so appended runs remain a valid file.

concepts.name: Following links and pagination
concepts.summary: Crawl beyond the first page with response.follow and follow_all, separate callbacks per page type, and pass data with cb_kwargs.
concepts.why: Real crawls go from list pages to detail pages and on to the next page of the list, and Scrapy's request model makes that natural.
concepts.body:
To crawl further, a callback yields **requests**. The convenient way is `response.follow(url, callback=...)`:

- It accepts relative URLs (`/page/2/`, which leave out the site) and combines them with the current page's URL.
- It also accepts a selector for an `<a>` element directly: `response.follow(a_selector, ...)`.
- `response.follow_all(css="li.next a", callback=self.parse)` creates requests for every match.

The callback defaults to `self.parse`. Use **different callbacks for different kinds of page**. On a list page, `parse` yields requests to the detail pages with `callback=self.parse_author`, and a request for the next list page with `callback=self.parse`.

Long lists are usually split across numbered pages, which is called **pagination**; following the "next" link handles it.

**Skipping duplicates**: Scrapy computes a short code, a **fingerprint**, from each request and drops requests it has already seen. So following the same author link from many quotes fetches it once. Pass `dont_filter=True` to skip that check when needed.

To pass data from one page to the next, use `cb_kwargs={"category": name}`: the values arrive as keyword arguments of the callback. That's the clean replacement for stuffing data into `request.meta`.

Pagination ends naturally when there's no next link. Guard against crawls that go too deep or never end with `DEPTH_LIMIT` or `CLOSESPIDER_PAGECOUNT`, and keep `allowed_domains` set so links to other sites are ignored.
takeaways: response.follow resolves relative URLs and accepts <a> selectors
Use separate callbacks per page type
Duplicate URLs are filtered automatically (dont_filter=True to override)
cb_kwargs passes data to the next callback
pitfalls: Building absolute URLs by string concatenation instead of response.follow / response.urljoin.

quiz.q: Twenty quotes link to the same author page. How many times does Scrapy download it by default?
quiz.explain: Scrapy's duplicate check drops requests whose fingerprint it has already seen.

concepts.name: Exploring pages in scrapy shell
concepts.summary: Use scrapy shell to fetch a page and try selectors interactively before putting them in a spider.
concepts.why: Developing selectors interactively is far faster than rerunning a whole crawl after every tweak.
concepts.body:
`scrapy shell "https://quotes.toscrape.com/"` downloads the page the way your spider would (with the same settings and headers, when run inside a project) and opens an interactive Python console, the **scrapy shell** (IPython if installed), with these objects ready:

- `response`: the downloaded page; try `response.css(...)` and `response.xpath(...)` right away.
- `request`, `settings`, `spider`, `crawler`.
- `fetch(url_or_request)`: download another page and replace `response`.
- `view(response)`: open the response in your browser **exactly as Scrapy received it**. That's the fastest way to see whether data is missing because JavaScript adds it only in the browser.
- `shelp()`: list the available objects and shortcuts.

You can also open it on a saved file (`scrapy shell ./page.html`) to work offline.

Inside a running spider, `from scrapy.shell import inspect_response` and a call to `inspect_response(response, self)` in a callback drops you into the scrapy shell at exactly that point, with the live response. That's great for **debugging**, hunting down why a page behaves differently from what you expected.

A related command, `scrapy fetch --nolog URL`, prints the page as Scrapy sees it, and `scrapy view URL` opens it in a browser.

Workflow: explore in scrapy shell, copy the selector into the spider, then run the spider on a few pages with `-s CLOSESPIDER_ITEMCOUNT=5` to check the output.
concepts.code:
# $ scrapy shell "https://quotes.toscrape.com/"
>>> response.status
200
>>> response.css("title::text").get()
'Quotes to Scrape'
>>> q = response.css("div.quote")[0]
>>> q.css("small.author::text").get()
'Albert Einstein'
>>> q.css("a.tag::text").getall()
['change', 'deep-thoughts', 'thinking', 'world']
>>> fetch("https://quotes.toscrape.com/page/2/")
>>> response.url
'https://quotes.toscrape.com/page/2/'
>>> view(response)          # opens the downloaded HTML in your browser
True
takeaways: scrapy shell URL gives you response, fetch() and view()
view(response) shows the page as Scrapy got it, without JavaScript
inspect_response(response, self) opens scrapy shell inside a callback
Develop selectors in scrapy shell, then paste them into the spider
pitfalls: Testing selectors only in the browser's developer tools, which show the page after JavaScript changed it, instead of on the raw response.

quiz.q: Selectors that work in Chrome's developer tools return nothing in Scrapy. Which scrapy shell helper helps most?
quiz.explain: view() shows the HTML Scrapy actually received, revealing content that JavaScript adds later in the browser.

concepts.name: Items and ItemLoaders
concepts.summary: Declare the fields of your items with scrapy.Item or dataclasses, and fill them cleanly with ItemLoader input and output processors.
concepts.why: Declared item fields catch typos and document your data, and loaders keep cleaning logic out of callbacks.
concepts.body:
Plain dicts work, but larger projects declare **item types** that list their fields. Scrapy supports, through the `itemadapter` library:

- `scrapy.Item` subclasses with `scrapy.Field()` attributes: assigning a field that wasn't declared raises `KeyError`, which catches typos.
- **dataclasses** and attrs classes, giving type hints and defaults.

Pipelines and exporters handle all of them the same way through `ItemAdapter(item)`.

An **ItemLoader** separates *where* data comes from and *how* it's cleaned:

- `loader = ItemLoader(item=Product(), response=response)` (or `selector=` for one part of the page).
- `loader.add_css("name", "h1::text")`, `add_xpath(...)`, `add_value("url", response.url)`; each call can add several values to a field.
- `loader.load_item()` returns the filled item.

Every value passes through cleaning functions (from the `itemloaders.processors` module) in two stages:

- **Input processors** run on each extracted value as it's added: `MapCompose(str.strip, to_float)` applies the functions in order and drops `None` results.
- **Output processors** run once on the collected list when loading: `TakeFirst()` returns the first non-empty value, `Join(", ")` joins them.

Set them per field (`name_in`, `price_out` attributes on a loader subclass, or `Field(input_processor=...)`) and set `default_output_processor = TakeFirst()`, since otherwise every field ends up a list.

Loaders shine on sites with many similar pages; for a quick spider, plain dicts with careful selectors are fine.
concepts.code:
from dataclasses import dataclass from itemloaders.processors import MapCompose, TakeFirst, Join from scrapy.http import HtmlResponse from scrapy.loader import ItemLoader @dataclass class Product: name: str | None = None price: float | None = None tags: str | None = None class ProductLoader(ItemLoader): default_item_class = Product default_output_processor = TakeFirst() name_in = MapCompose(str.strip) price_in = MapCompose(lambda s: s.replace("EUR", "").strip(), float) tags_out = Join(", ") body = b'

Kettle

29.90 EURhomesteel' response = HtmlResponse(url="https://shop.example/p/1", body=body, encoding="utf-8") loader = ProductLoader(response=response) loader.add_css("name", "h1::text") loader.add_css("price", "span.price::text") loader.add_css("tags", "a.tag::text") print(loader.load_item()) # Product(name='Kettle', price=29.9, tags='home, steel')
takeaways: scrapy.Item, dataclasses and attrs all work as items via ItemAdapter
ItemLoader: add_css / add_xpath / add_value, then load_item()
Input processors clean each value; output processors combine the list
Set default_output_processor = TakeFirst() to avoid list fields
pitfalls: Forgetting an output processor and exporting every field as a one-element list.

quiz.q: What does MapCompose(str.strip, float) do as an input processor?
options: Joins all values into a float
Validates that values are floats without converting
Strips and converts the first value only
Applies str.strip then float to each extracted value
quiz.explain: MapCompose applies its functions in sequence to every input value.

concepts.name: Item pipelines
concepts.summary: Check, clean, deduplicate and store items in pipeline classes enabled and ordered through ITEM_PIPELINES.
concepts.why: Pipelines keep storage and checking out of spiders, so the same logic applies to every spider in a project.
concepts.body:
After a callback yields an item, it passes through the **item pipelines**: classes with a `process_item(self, item)` method, switched on in settings:

`ITEM_PIPELINES = {"bookstore.pipelines.ValidatePipeline": 100, "bookstore.pipelines.PostgresPipeline": 800}`

The numbers (0 to 1000) set the order: **lower runs first**. Each `process_item` must either **return the item** (possibly changed) to pass it on, or **raise `DropItem`** to discard it, which is logged and counted in the crawl's statistics.

Typical pipelines, in order:

- Validation: drop items missing required fields.
- Cleaning: prices to numbers, dates to a standard format such as `2025-03-14`.
- Removing duplicates: keep a set of keys already seen and drop repeats.
- Storage: write to a **database** (a program that stores data and finds it again quickly) or send to another service.

Start and end hooks: `open_spider()` and `close_spider()` run once per crawl, the place to open and close database connections. A `from_crawler(cls, crawler)` class method gives access to settings (such as connection details) and the crawler.

Use `ItemAdapter(item)` to read and write fields, so the pipeline works with dicts, Items and dataclasses alike.

`process_item` may also be an `async def` method, which suits database libraries written for async code. Older Scrapy versions passed a `spider` argument to these methods; current versions use `from_crawler` and `crawler.spider` instead.
takeaways: process_item returns the item to pass it on or raises DropItem
ITEM_PIPELINES numbers set the order: lower first
open_spider / close_spider manage resources; from_crawler reads settings
Use ItemAdapter to support every item type
pitfalls: Forgetting to return the item, so every later pipeline and the feed receive None.

quiz.q: Pipelines A: 300 and B: 100 are enabled. In what order do they see an item?
quiz.explain: Lower numbers run first, so B (100) processes the item before A (300).

concepts.name: Settings and polite crawling
concepts.summary: Configure robots.txt obedience, delays, concurrency, AutoThrottle, user agent and the HTTP cache through Scrapy settings.
concepts.why: Crawling too aggressively gets you blocked and can hurt the sites you depend on; Scrapy has the knobs built in.
concepts.body:
Settings come from several levels, lowest to highest priority: Scrapy's defaults, the project's `settings.py`, the spider's `custom_settings` dict, and the terminal (`-s NAME=value`).

Politeness and identity:

- `ROBOTSTXT_OBEY = True`: respect the site's **robots.txt** file, which says what automated programs may fetch (a new project's settings switch it on; the built-in default is False).
- `USER_AGENT`: identify your bot, ideally with a contact URL.
- `DOWNLOAD_DELAY = 1`: seconds between requests to the same site, varied randomly between 0.5x and 1.5x by default (`DOWNLOAD_DELAY_JITTER = 0.5`; older versions used `RANDOMIZE_DOWNLOAD_DELAY`).
- `CONCURRENT_REQUESTS` (default 16 overall) and `CONCURRENT_REQUESTS_PER_DOMAIN` (default 8; a new project's settings use 1).

**AutoThrottle** (`AUTOTHROTTLE_ENABLED = True`) adjusts the delay to how quickly the server answers, aiming at `AUTOTHROTTLE_TARGET_CONCURRENCY` requests in progress per server at once. It slows down automatically when the site does, which usually beats a fixed guess.

Development helpers:

- `HTTPCACHE_ENABLED = True` saves responses on disk and reuses them (a **cache**), so reruns while you tweak your parsing don't hit the site.
- `CLOSESPIDER_ITEMCOUNT` / `CLOSESPIDER_PAGECOUNT` stop early.
- `LOG_LEVEL = "INFO"` cuts noise.

Read settings in code with `self.settings.getint("DOWNLOAD_DELAY")` in a spider, or `crawler.settings` in other components. `scrapy settings --get NAME` shows the value in effect inside a project.
concepts.code:
# settings.py
BOT_NAME = "bookstore"
USER_AGENT = "bookstore-bot/1.0 (+https://example.com/bot)"
ROBOTSTXT_OBEY = True

CONCURRENT_REQUESTS_PER_DOMAIN = 2
DOWNLOAD_DELAY = 0.5

AUTOTHROTTLE_ENABLED = True
AUTOTHROTTLE_START_DELAY = 1
AUTOTHROTTLE_MAX_DELAY = 30
AUTOTHROTTLE_TARGET_CONCURRENCY = 1.0

HTTPCACHE_ENABLED = True          # dev only: reuse downloaded pages
HTTPCACHE_EXPIRATION_SECS = 3600
FEED_EXPORT_ENCODING = "utf-8"

# One-off overrides from the command line:
# $ scrapy crawl books -s LOG_LEVEL=INFO -s CLOSESPIDER_ITEMCOUNT=20
takeaways: Priority: defaults < settings.py < custom_settings < -s in the terminal
Obey robots.txt, identify yourself, and limit requests per site
AutoThrottle adapts delays to how fast the server answers
HTTPCACHE_ENABLED speeds up reruns during development
pitfalls: Leaving HTTPCACHE_ENABLED on in real crawls and scraping outdated pages.

quiz.q: A spider sets custom_settings = {'DOWNLOAD_DELAY': 2} and you run with -s DOWNLOAD_DELAY=0.5. Which delay applies?
quiz.explain: Command-line settings have the highest priority.

concepts.name: CrawlSpider and link extraction rules
concepts.summary: Crawl whole sections of a site by describing them with CrawlSpider, Rule and LinkExtractor patterns.
concepts.why: Many crawls are 'follow these kinds of links, parse those kinds of pages', which rules express in a few lines.
concepts.body:
`CrawlSpider` is a Spider subclass driven by **rules** that describe what to follow, instead of you writing the following yourself. Each `Rule` wraps a **`LinkExtractor`** that finds links in every response, plus what to do with them:

- `LinkExtractor(allow=r"/catalogue/category/")`: regular expressions the URL must match; `deny=` excludes; `restrict_css=` / `restrict_xpaths=` look for links only in one part of the page, such as the main content or the page-number links.
- `Rule(extractor, callback="parse_book")`: parse the linked pages with that method.
- `follow=True` (the default when there's no callback): keep applying the rules to those pages too.

Rules are tried in order, and a link is handled by the **first** rule that matches it, so put specific rules before general ones.

A typical setup has one rule that follows category and next-page links without a callback, and one rule that sends product pages to `parse_item`.

The crucial gotcha: **don't define a method called `parse`** in a CrawlSpider. CrawlSpider uses `parse` itself to apply the rules; replacing it silently switches the crawling off. Name callbacks `parse_item` or similar. To also parse the start pages, override `parse_start_url`.

`LinkExtractor` is useful outside CrawlSpider too: `LinkExtractor(...).extract_links(response)` returns `Link` objects with `.url` and `.text`, without duplicates and with full URLs.

Sites often publish a `sitemap.xml` file listing all their pages. `SitemapSpider` crawls from it, which is often the most efficient way to reach every page.
concepts.code:
from scrapy.linkextractors import LinkExtractor
from scrapy.spiders import CrawlSpider, Rule

class BooksSpider(CrawlSpider):
    name = "books"
    allowed_domains = ["books.toscrape.com"]
    start_urls = ["https://books.toscrape.com/"]

    rules = (
        # book detail pages -> parse_book (and don't follow further)
        Rule(LinkExtractor(restrict_css="article.product_pod h3"),
             callback="parse_book", follow=False),
        # category and pagination pages -> just follow
        Rule(LinkExtractor(restrict_css=["ul.nav-list", "li.next"])),
    )

    def parse_book(self, response):          # never name this "parse"
        yield {
            "title": response.css("div.product_main h1::text").get(),
            "price": response.css("p.price_color::text").get(),
            "url": response.url,
        }
takeaways: CrawlSpider + Rule(LinkExtractor(...)) crawls by description
allow/deny patterns and restrict_css focus link extraction
The first matching rule handles a link: order matters
Never override parse in a CrawlSpider
pitfalls: Naming a CrawlSpider callback parse and wondering why no links are followed.

quiz.q: Why must a CrawlSpider not define its own parse method?
options: Rules only call methods starting with rule_
It makes the spider run twice
CrawlSpider uses parse internally to apply the rules
quiz.explain: Overriding parse replaces the logic that extracts links and applies rules.

concepts.name: Requests, forms and JSON APIs
concepts.summary: Build your own Requests with headers and methods, submit HTML forms with form2request, and use JSON APIs.
concepts.why: Logins, search forms and the JSON addresses behind modern pages are where most valuable data hides.
concepts.body:
Besides `response.follow`, you can build requests yourself: `scrapy.Request(url, method="POST", headers={...}, body=..., callback=..., cb_kwargs=..., meta=...)`. To send form data you already know, `FormRequest(url, formdata={...})` encodes it the way a browser would.

**HTML forms** are the boxes and buttons where you type a login or a search. They usually contain hidden fields you must send back, such as a **CSRF token**: a one-time code the site puts in the form to check that the submission really came from its own page. Recent Scrapy versions recommend the **form2request** library for this (`pip install form2request`). `form2request(response.css("form#login"), {"username": "u", "password": "p"})` reads the form, keeps its hidden fields, fills in your values, and works out the URL and method the form submits to; `.to_scrapy(callback=...)` turns the result into a Scrapy request. Older code uses `FormRequest.from_response(response, formdata=...)`, which does the same but is being phased out.

Cookies are handled automatically, so after you sign in, later requests in the same crawl stay signed in.

**JSON APIs**: many pages load their data from separate addresses that return JSON. A service that hands out data to programs like this is an **API**. You can find these requests in the network tab of your browser's developer tools, and call them directly:

- `response.json()` turns a JSON response body into Python dicts and lists.
- `scrapy.http.JsonRequest(url, data={...})` sends a JSON body with the right headers (as a POST when `data` is given).
- For results split into pages, work out the next page from the JSON (`page + 1`, or a "next" value it gives you) and yield a new request until the results run out.

APIs are usually faster, more stable and lighter on the server than HTML pages. Still respect the site's terms, its login requirements and its limits on how often you may call it.
takeaways: scrapy.Request takes method, headers, body, callback, cb_kwargs
form2request builds a submission from a real form, keeping hidden fields
Cookies are kept across requests automatically
response.json() and JsonRequest for JSON APIs
pitfalls: Posting login data with a plain FormRequest and missing the page's CSRF token.

quiz.q: Why build a login request from the page's <form> instead of posting the fields yourself?
options: It includes the form's hidden fields (like CSRF tokens) and its real action and method
quiz.explain: Reading the real form submits required hidden inputs along with your values.

concepts.name: Downloader and spider middlewares
concepts.summary: Hook into every request and response with downloader middlewares (headers, proxies, ready-made responses) and know where spider middlewares fit.
concepts.why: Proxies, login headers, changing user agents and custom caching are all built as middlewares in real Scrapy projects.
concepts.body:
Inside Scrapy, a central **engine** passes each request to the downloader, which fetches it. On the way, requests travel through the **downloader middlewares**: classes plugged in between that can look at, change or replace what passes. Responses travel back through them in reverse order. Each middleware has optional methods:

- `process_request(request, spider)`: return `None` to continue, a `Response` to skip the download entirely (for example an answer already saved in a cache), a new `Request` to schedule instead, or raise `IgnoreRequest`.
- `process_response(request, response, spider)`: return the response (possibly replaced) or a `Request` to try differently.
- `process_exception(request, exception, spider)`: handle download errors such as timeouts.

Enable them with `DOWNLOADER_MIDDLEWARES = {"proj.middlewares.ProxyMiddleware": 543}`. The number places it among the built-ins in `DOWNLOADER_MIDDLEWARES_BASE` (robots.txt at 100, user agent at 500, retry at 550, redirect at 600, cookies at 700, HTTP proxy at 750, cache at 900). Lower numbers are closer to the engine: their `process_request` runs **first** and their `process_response` runs **last**. Set a built-in to `None` to switch it off.

Common uses: sending requests through a **proxy** (a middle server that forwards your traffic) via `request.meta["proxy"]`, adding login headers, rotating user agents, and spotting "you are blocked" pages so they can be retried.

**Spider middlewares** sit between the engine and your spider's callbacks, handling responses going in and items and requests coming out (`process_spider_output`, `process_start`). The built-ins filter error responses, enforce depth limits and add the referring page's URL to requests; custom ones are rarer than downloader middlewares.

Write `from_crawler(cls, crawler)` to read settings and subscribe to Scrapy's events.
takeaways: process_request: None continues, Response short-circuits, Request reschedules
process_response can replace the response or return a new Request
Order numbers: lower = closer to the engine (request first, response last)
Spider middlewares wrap callbacks; downloader middlewares wrap downloads
pitfalls: Returning a retried Request without dont_filter=True, so the duplicate filter silently drops it.

quiz.q: A downloader middleware's process_request returns a Response object. What happens?
options: The download is skipped and that response goes back through process_response methods
quiz.explain: Returning a Response short-circuits the downloader, which is how caching middlewares work.

concepts.name: Errors, retries and errbacks
concepts.summary: Handle failed requests with errbacks, control retries and HTTP error filtering, and keep partial failures visible.
concepts.why: Networks fail, servers return 500s and pages vanish, and a crawler must cope without silently losing data.
concepts.body:
By default, responses whose status code isn't in the 200s never reach your callback: a spider middleware, **HttpErrorMiddleware**, drops them. To receive them anyway, set `handle_httpstatus_list = [404]` on the spider, `meta={"handle_httpstatus_list": [404]}` on a request, or `HTTPERROR_ALLOWED_CODES` for the whole project.

The **RetryMiddleware** retries connection errors, timeouts (no answer within the time limit) and the codes in `RETRY_HTTP_CODES` (500, 502, 503, 504, 522, 524, 408, 429) up to `RETRY_TIMES` (default 2) extra times. Adjust it per request with `meta={"max_retry_times": 5}`, or turn it off with `dont_retry`. To retry from your own code (say, an error page sent with status 200), use `get_retry_request(response.request, spider=self, reason="empty page")`, which respects the same limits and statistics.

An **errback** is a function called when a request fails for good: `scrapy.Request(url, callback=..., errback=self.on_error)`. It receives a Twisted `Failure` object (Twisted is the networking library Scrapy is built on):

- `failure.check(HttpError)`, `DNSLookupError`, `TimeoutError` identify the cause.
- `failure.request` is the failed request; for HttpError, `failure.value.response` holds the response.

Use errbacks to log failures, record failed URLs as items to process again later, or yield other requests instead.

At the end of a crawl, check the **stats** Scrapy prints (`downloader/response_status_count/404`, `retry/max_reached`, `log_count/ERROR`). A crawl that "finished" with thousands of errors is a failure; set up alerts on these numbers.
takeaways: Error statuses are filtered out unless allowed via handle_httpstatus_list
RetryMiddleware retries network errors and 5xx/429; tune RETRY_TIMES
get_retry_request retries from callbacks with the same limits
An errback receives a Failure; check its type and log or record it
pitfalls: Expecting a 404 page in the callback without handle_httpstatus_list, and never seeing it.

quiz.q: Your callback never sees 404 responses. Why?
options: The HttpError middleware filters non-2xx responses unless they're explicitly allowed
quiz.explain: Only successful responses reach callbacks by default; allow specific codes with handle_httpstatus_list.

concepts.name: JavaScript-rendered pages
concepts.summary: Handle pages whose content JavaScript adds in the browser: find the underlying API, read embedded JSON, or render with scrapy-playwright.
concepts.why: Many modern sites send nearly empty HTML and fill it in with JavaScript, and the right technique decides between a fast crawler and a slow, fragile one.
concepts.body:
Scrapy downloads HTML; it doesn't run JavaScript. If `view(response)` in the shell shows the page without the data, the content is added later in the browser. In order of preference:

- **Find where the data comes from.** Open the network tab of the browser's developer tools and filter by "Fetch/XHR" (the requests JavaScript makes). Look for responses containing your data as JSON.
- Then repeat that request in Scrapy: the same URL, the same settings after the `?` in it, and any headers that matter. Read the result with `response.json()`. This is usually the fastest and most robust option.
- **Read the embedded starting data.** The JavaScript frameworks sites are built with often put the starting data right into the HTML: in `<script id="__NEXT_DATA__" type="application/json">`, as `window.__INITIAL_STATE__ = {...}`, or as JSON-LD (a JSON description of a product or article in a script tag). Extract the script's text with a selector and `json.loads` it. When it's written as JavaScript rather than strict JSON, a regular expression or the chompjs library helps.
- **Render the page** in a **headless browser** (a real browser run by code, without a window) via **scrapy-playwright**. Install it, configure its download handler and the asyncio reactor, and mark requests with `meta={"playwright": True}`. You can wait for elements to appear, click and scroll. Rendering is hundreds of times slower and heavier, so render only the pages that need it.

Hosted services for rendering and for getting past anti-bot protection exist too (for example Zyte API), plugged in as download handlers or middlewares.

Whatever you choose, keep the extraction code separate from the fetching, so that switching from rendered HTML to a discovered API later doesn't mean rewriting your parsing.
takeaways: Check view(response): missing data means JavaScript adds it in the browser
Best: call the JSON API the page uses
Next: read embedded JSON from script tags
Last resort: render with scrapy-playwright, only for pages that need it
pitfalls: Rendering every page in a browser when one JSON address would return all the data.

quiz.q: Which approach is usually fastest and most stable for a JavaScript-heavy site?
options: Calling the JSON endpoint the page itself uses
quiz.explain: The JSON API returns structured data directly, without running a browser.

concepts.name: Running from scripts and in production
concepts.summary: Run crawls from Python with CrawlerProcess, save and resume long crawls with JOBDIR, and deploy spiders to run on a schedule or on Scrapyd.
concepts.why: Crawlers in real use run unattended on schedules, must survive restarts and report what happened.
concepts.body:
Besides `scrapy crawl`, you can start crawls from Python. **`AsyncCrawlerProcess`** (or the older-style `CrawlerProcess`, whose methods return Twisted Deferreds instead of coroutines) starts the **reactor**, Twisted's loop that runs everything, then runs one or more spiders and waits until they finish: `process = AsyncCrawlerProcess(settings); process.crawl(MySpider, category="books"); process.start()`. Keyword arguments become spider attributes (the same as `-a category=books` in the terminal). Use `get_project_settings()` to load the project's settings.py. If your program already runs its own asyncio loop, `AsyncCrawlerRunner` / `CrawlerRunner` let you start crawls without Scrapy starting the reactor for you.

The reactor can't be restarted inside one running program, so to run crawls repeatedly (from a scheduler, say), start a fresh Python **process** (a separately running copy of the program) per crawl, for example with `subprocess` or a job runner.

**Pause and resume**: `scrapy crawl big -s JOBDIR=crawls/big-1` saves the queue of waiting requests and the fingerprints of requests already seen to disk. Stop with a single Ctrl-C, which lets Scrapy finish cleanly, and rerun the same command to continue. The saved requests must be storable on disk, so their callbacks must be spider methods.

Ways to **deploy** a crawler, that is, put it where it runs on its own:

- Scheduled jobs: package the project (for example as a Docker **container**) and start it on a timer, with a **cron job**, Kubernetes CronJobs or Airflow. Simple and common.
- **Scrapyd**, a server program that runs in the background; you upload projects to it and start spiders through HTTP requests.
- Hosted platforms such as Zyte Scrapy Cloud.

In every case, send the logs and the final stats (item counts, error counts, why the crawl finished) to whatever system you use to watch your services.
takeaways: AsyncCrawlerProcess (or CrawlerProcess) runs spiders from a script and waits
Keyword arguments to crawl() become spider arguments
The reactor can't restart: one process per crawl run
JOBDIR saves the queue and seen requests for pause/resume
pitfalls: Calling process.start() twice in one process and hitting ReactorNotRestartable.

quiz.q: What does setting JOBDIR enable?
options: Pausing and resuming a crawl with its queue and seen requests persisted
quiz.explain: JOBDIR stores the waiting requests and the duplicate filter's memory on disk so a stopped crawl can resume.

concepts.name: Architecture: engine, scheduler and data flow
concepts.summary: How the engine, scheduler, downloader, middlewares, spiders and pipelines interact, and how request deduplication and priorities work.
concepts.why: Understanding how data flows lets you put custom logic in the right place and track down ordering, duplicate and speed problems.
concepts.body:
Scrapy's core is an **engine** that reacts to events (a response arriving, a download slot freeing up) rather than running steps in a fixed order. It runs on Twisted's reactor, which in current versions runs on asyncio's event loop. The path of each request:

- The spider's `start()` yields the first requests; the engine passes them to the **scheduler**, which holds the requests waiting to be downloaded.
- The scheduler asks the **dupefilter** whether the request was seen before (by its fingerprint: method, normalised URL, body), and queues new requests by priority. `Request(priority=10)` jumps ahead; `dont_filter=True` skips the duplicate check.
- When the downloader has free slots, the engine takes the next request from the scheduler and sends it through the **downloader middlewares** to the **downloader**. The downloader keeps one **slot** per site, which enforces that site's concurrency limit and delay.
- The response comes back through the downloader middlewares, then through the **spider middlewares** into your **callback**.
- Items the callback yields go to the **item pipelines**; requests go back to the scheduler.

All of this runs in a single thread and nothing is allowed to wait. A callback that blocks (a `time.sleep`, a database call that waits for its answer, heavy computation) stalls the entire crawl, not just that request.

The default queues are **LIFO** (last in, first out), so the crawl goes deep first, which keeps memory low for typical crawls. Requests are scheduled, not run in the order you yield them, so the order between pages is never guaranteed.

**Signals** (`spider_opened`, `item_scraped`, `request_dropped`, `spider_closed`) and the **stats collector** report these events, and extensions subscribe to them. That's how built-ins like CloseSpider, AutoThrottle and the memory usage monitor work.
takeaways: Flow: spider -> scheduler -> downloader (via middlewares) -> spider -> pipelines
The dupefilter drops repeated request fingerprints; priority reorders
Single-threaded event loop: blocking code stalls the whole crawl
Signals and stats expose every step to extensions
pitfalls: Calling a blocking download library (like Requests) or time.sleep inside a callback, freezing every other request.

quiz.q: A callback runs a 2-second synchronous database query per page. What's the effect?
options: The whole crawl stalls for 2 seconds each time, since everything shares one event loop
Scrapy moves it to a thread automatically
quiz.explain: Callbacks run on the reactor thread, so blocking calls stop all other processing.

concepts.name: async callbacks and asyncio integration
concepts.summary: Write async def callbacks and pipelines, await asyncio libraries under the asyncio reactor, and bridge Twisted Deferreds.
concepts.why: Modern Scrapy code awaits async database libraries and APIs directly, which requires understanding how the asyncio reactor fits in.
concepts.body:
Scrapy supports **coroutines** in many places: callbacks (`async def parse(self, response)`, using `yield` to make an async generator), the spider's `async def start()`, item pipelines' `process_item`, and downloader middleware methods.

Inside them you can `await`:

- asyncio libraries (an async database driver, an async HTTP client for a side call), because Scrapy runs Twisted on the **asyncio reactor** (`TWISTED_REACTOR = "twisted.internet.asyncioreactor.AsyncioSelectorReactor"`), the default in current versions.
- Twisted Deferreds, converted with `scrapy.utils.defer.maybe_deferred_to_future(d)` so they're awaitable under asyncio.

An async callback that yields lets you do things like enrich an item from an API before yielding it, without blocking other requests: while one coroutine awaits, the event loop serves others.

Caveats:

- Awaiting inside a callback delays that callback's output; it doesn't add concurrency by itself. For many independent fetches, yield more Scrapy requests instead of awaiting in a loop.
- The reactor must be installed before anything imports `twisted.internet.reactor`; installing it late raises an error about the wrong reactor.
- CPU-heavy work still blocks the loop; offload it with `asyncio.to_thread` or a process pool.

Prefer Scrapy's own requests for crawling (they get throttling, retries, middlewares and stats); use direct awaits for auxiliary calls like databases or caches.
concepts.code:
import asyncio
import scrapy

async def lookup_country(author):             # stand-in for an async DB/API call
    await asyncio.sleep(0.05)
    return {"Albert Einstein": "DE", "Jane Austen": "GB"}.get(author)

class AsyncQuotesSpider(scrapy.Spider):
    name = "async_quotes"
    start_urls = ["https://quotes.toscrape.com/"]

    async def parse(self, response):
        authors = response.css("small.author::text").getall()
        countries = await asyncio.gather(*(lookup_country(a) for a in authors))
        for author, country in zip(authors, countries):
            yield {"author": author, "country": country}

class SaveToDbPipeline:
    async def process_item(self, item):
        await asyncio.sleep(0.01)                # e.g. await db.insert(item)
        return item

# TWISTED_REACTOR = "twisted.internet.asyncioreactor.AsyncioSelectorReactor"  (default)
takeaways: Callbacks, start(), pipelines and middlewares can be coroutines
The asyncio reactor lets you await asyncio libraries
maybe_deferred_to_future makes Twisted Deferreds awaitable
Awaiting doesn't add crawl concurrency: yield Requests for that
pitfalls: Fetching hundreds of pages with an async HTTP client inside one callback, bypassing throttling, retries and stats.

quiz.q: Why should crawling still use Scrapy Requests rather than awaiting an async HTTP client in callbacks?
options: Scrapy Requests get scheduling, throttling, retries, middlewares and stats
await is not allowed in callbacks
It's required by the asyncio reactor
quiz.explain: Direct awaits bypass the whole download pipeline that makes crawls polite and observable.

concepts.name: Broad crawls and scaling out
concepts.summary: Tune Scrapy for crawling many sites: concurrency, breadth-first order, DownloaderAwarePriorityQueue, memory limits and crawling on several machines.
concepts.why: Crawling thousands of sites is a different job from scraping one, and defaults tuned for one site hold it back.
concepts.body:
A **broad crawl** visits many sites, often without knowing them in advance. Scrapy's defaults are tuned for crawling a single site, so the limits shift from politeness to raw speed and memory. Scrapy's guide recommends:

- Raise overall concurrency: set `CONCURRENT_REQUESTS` close to `CONCURRENT_REQUESTS_PER_DOMAIN` times the number of sites being crawled at once, as your machine's processor and memory allow. Raise `SCRAPER_SLOT_MAX_ACTIVE_SIZE` when more concurrency stops helping.
- Keep the scheduler aware of sites: `SCHEDULER_PRIORITY_QUEUE = "scrapy.pqueues.DownloaderAwarePriorityQueue"` (the default in current versions; older ones needed it set) picks requests for sites with free download slots, so one slow site can't hold everything up.
- Speed up DNS, the lookup that turns a site's name into its numeric address: use a local caching DNS server and a larger `REACTOR_THREADPOOL_MAXSIZE`, since these lookups run in threads.
- Make bad responses cheaper: reduce or switch off retries, lower `DOWNLOAD_TIMEOUT`, set `REDIRECT_ENABLED = False` unless you need redirects, and cap sizes with `DOWNLOAD_MAXSIZE`.

Consider **breadth-first order**: `DEPTH_PRIORITY = 1` with FIFO (first in, first out) queues, `SCHEDULER_DISK_QUEUE = "scrapy.squeues.PickleFifoDiskQueue"` and `SCHEDULER_MEMORY_QUEUE = "scrapy.squeues.FifoMemoryQueue"`. It visits many sites a little before going deep, and the docs suggest trying it when memory runs short. `JOBDIR` keeps the queue on disk.

Guard memory and endless link traps with `MEMUSAGE_LIMIT_MB` and `DEPTH_LIMIT`. Calendars with a "next month" link forever, and URLs carrying a fresh visitor ID on every link, are classic traps.

When one process isn't enough, spread the crawl over several. Run several Scrapy processes that share **one central queue and dupefilter**, typically with the scrapy-redis extension, or split the URLs (for example by site) across independent crawlers.

At this scale politeness still applies per site: keep obeying robots.txt and per-site limits.
concepts.code:
# settings.py for a broad crawl
CONCURRENT_REQUESTS = 200                  # ~2 per domain x 100 domains
CONCURRENT_REQUESTS_PER_DOMAIN = 2
SCHEDULER_PRIORITY_QUEUE = "scrapy.pqueues.DownloaderAwarePriorityQueue"
REACTOR_THREADPOOL_MAXSIZE = 20

# breadth-first order
DEPTH_PRIORITY = 1
SCHEDULER_DISK_QUEUE = "scrapy.squeues.PickleFifoDiskQueue"
SCHEDULER_MEMORY_QUEUE = "scrapy.squeues.FifoMemoryQueue"
DEPTH_LIMIT = 3

REDIRECT_ENABLED = False
RETRY_ENABLED = False
DOWNLOAD_TIMEOUT = 15
DOWNLOAD_MAXSIZE = 5 * 1024 * 1024     # skip responses over 5 MB
MEMUSAGE_LIMIT_MB = 2048
LOG_LEVEL = "INFO"
ROBOTSTXT_OBEY = True

# $ scrapy crawl broad -s JOBDIR=crawls/broad-1
takeaways: Raise overall concurrency toward per-site limit x number of sites
DownloaderAwarePriorityQueue keeps slow sites from hogging the queue
DEPTH_PRIORITY=1 + FIFO queues = breadth-first crawling
Scale out with a shared queue and dupefilter (e.g. scrapy-redis)
pitfalls: Running a broad crawl with single-site defaults, so it dives deep into the first few sites while most sites wait.

quiz.q: Which settings give breadth-first crawl order?
options: DEPTH_PRIORITY = 1 with FIFO disk and memory queues
quiz.explain: Positive depth priority deprioritizes deeper requests, and FIFO queues process them in arrival order.
